issues.final_text: Опущены также второй сон Александра и основание Триполиса из трёх деревень. Во сне сатир протягивает Александру сыр (tyrum, греч. τυρός), Александр бросает его и растаптывает, а толкователи объясняют: Тир (Tyrum) скоро будет попран ногами царя.
issues.evidence:
The reviewer is right on the substance. Two details in the reviewer's evidence are wrong, and the proposed wording can be made more exact.

1) VALERIUS (Kübler 1888, p. 47, lines 3-9; checked in both archive.org scans and on the page image). This is chapter 36 in Kübler's numbering, which equals Müller XXXV:
"His igitur incentivis exstimulatus Alexander inruptionem oppidi acrius agitabat et rursus in somnio Satyrum conspicatur assem sibi tyrum porrigentem eumque proiectum sese pedibus protrivisse. Quod interpretibus haud difficile in enodando fuit. Tyrum enim proteri mox pedibus habere principis respondere."
So Valerius has only the cheese: tyrum, a Greek loanword. The interpreters read it as 'Tyrum ... proteri mox pedibus' (Tyre is soon to be trampled underfoot). Valerius has no division of satyr into sa-Tyros and no 'Tyre is yours'. The pun works on tyrum (cheese) against Tyrum (Tyre); in the accusative the two words are spelled alike. 'rursus in somnio' marks this as the second dream; the first is the warning against going as his own envoy (p. 46, 13-15). So 'второй сон' fits the earlier sentence of note 53.

Apparatus to line 5, from the page image: "5 in somnis Eberh. saturum A. saturnum P. assem sibi τυροῦ porrigentem Mai. assem sibi porrigentem P. caseum sibi porr. Eberh." To line 8: "habere Thielmann ... haberi A. P."
The reviewer is wrong on two points. (a) Mai printed the genitive τυροῦ, not τυρόν. (b) The reviewer leaves out the word 'assem', which is in Kübler's text and in both manuscripts A and P. P also drops 'tyrum'. Eberhard replaces the phrase with caseum. None of this changes the meaning ('cheese'), so the note can simply say 'сыр'.

2) α (Kroll 1926, p. 40, lines 4-9 = α 1.35.7-8; checked on the page image): "ὁρᾷ δὲ κατὰ τοὺς ὕπνους ἕνα ⟨τῶν⟩ τοῦ Διονύσου προπόλων Σάτυρον ἐπιδιδόντα αὐτῷ τυρόν, αὐτὸν δὲ λαβόντα τοῖς ποσὶν αὐτὸν συμπατεῖν ... 'Βασιλεῦ Ἀλέξανδρε, σοὶ Τύρος γίνεται ὑποχείριος διὰ τό σε τυρὸν τοῖς ποσὶ καταπεπατηκέναι.'"
Apparatus to line 8: "διὰ τὸν σατύριον A duo subsunt oracula, unum ad satyrum pertinens (σὰ Τύρος) alterum ad caseum, cf. B' Byz."
So the α text as Kroll prints it has the cheese. Only traces of the satyr pun remain: manuscript A's 'διὰ τὸν σατύριον' and the phrase 'σοὶ Τύρος'. Kroll takes these as signs that two interpretations were merged. Valerius kept only the cheese one.

3) PLUTARCH, Alex. 24.8-9 (Perrin, Loeb vol. VII, 1919, p. 292 Greek / p. 293 English; archive.org plutarchslives07plut; LacusCurtius). Greek: "Σάτυρος αὐτῷ φανεὶς ἐδόκει προσπαίζειν πόρρωθεν ... οἱ δὲ μάντεις τοὔνομα διαιροῦντες οὐκ ἀπιθάνως ἔφασαν αὐτῷ· 'Σὴ γενήσεται Τύρος.'" English: "The seers, dividing the word 'satyros' into two parts, said to him ... 'Tyre is to be thine.'" Plutarch has no cheese. Perrin's text reads Σή, not Σά; the form σὰ Τύρος appears in Kroll's apparatus. The sa-Tyros reading therefore comes from Plutarch, with a trace in α, and not from Valerius. Note 53 has mixed Plutarch's version into Valerius.

4) Wording. The reviewer's 'который тот растоптал' is unclear about who did the trampling, and the reviewer's text leaves out the interpreters' reading, which is the point of the dream. My wording follows Valerius: proiectum means 'бросает', pedibus protrivisse means 'растаптывает', and principis means 'царя'.

Optional extra sentence if you want to keep the information from the old note: «Игра «са-Тирос» (σάτυρος → σὰ Τύρος, «Тир твой») — у Плутарха (Alex. 24, 8–9); в α от неё остался лишь след (Kroll, p. 40, app. к стр. 8).»

The rest of note 53 matches Valerius:
- The oracle: "oraculi cuiusdam memores ... quod si rex urbem Tyriam invectus cum exercitu transivisset, fortuna tunc lapsum oppido minaretur" (46, 5-8).
- The envoy dream: "somniat admoneri sese, ne legationem sui Tyrum per sese faciat" (46, 13-14).
- The torture: "pergunt exigere tormentis, quisnam eorum ipse Alexander foret" (46, 28-47, 2).
- Tripolis: "Tres vero vicos, quorum navo auxilio ad operam bellicam usus erat, ad magnitudinem confrequentat urbis Tripolimque appellari iubet" (47, 11-14).
- The Epitome has no motive for the torture: "tormentis primum affectos crucibus affixerunt".

issues.final_text: Also omitted are Alexander's second dream and the founding of Tripolis from three villages. In the dream a satyr holds out a cheese to him (tyrum, Greek τυρός); Alexander throws it down and tramples it, and the interpreters explain that Tyre (Tyrum) will soon be trampled under the king's feet.
issues.evidence:
The evidence is the same as for issue 15. Valerius, Kübler p. 47, 4-9: "rursus in somnio Satyrum conspicatur assem sibi tyrum porrigentem eumque proiectum sese pedibus protrivisse. Quod interpretibus haud difficile in enodando fuit. Tyrum enim proteri mox pedibus habere principis respondere." There is no 'sa-Tyros' in Valerius. That pun is Plutarch's: Alex. 24.8-9, Perrin p. 292, "οἱ δὲ μάντεις τοὔνομα διαιροῦντες ... 'Σὴ γενήσεται Τύρος'", translated on p. 293 as "dividing the word 'satyros' into two parts". α (Kroll p. 40, 4-9) has the cheese (τυρόν ... συμπατεῖν; 'σοὶ Τύρος γίνεται ὑποχείριος διὰ τό σε τυρὸν τοῖς ποσὶ καταπεπατηκέναι'). Kroll's apparatus says two interpretations are merged there: 'unum ad satyrum pertinens (σὰ Τύρος) alterum ad caseum'.

The reviewer's EN fix is right in substance. Its only fault is that it leaves out how the interpreters read the dream ('Tyrum ... proteri mox pedibus'), and that reading is what makes the pun. 'Second dream' follows Valerius' 'rursus in somnio' and the envoy dream mentioned earlier in the note. 'Throws it down' renders proiectum, and 'king' renders principis.

Optional extra sentence: "The ‘sa-Tyros’ pun (σάτυρος → σὰ Τύρος, ‘Tyre is yours’) is Plutarch’s (Alex. 24.8–9); α keeps only a trace of it (Kroll, p. 40, app. to l. 8)."

The reviewer is wrong in one detail of the evidence for both issues: Mai's reading in Kübler's apparatus is τυροῦ (genitive), not τυρόν, as the page image shows.

The reviewer's evidence has an error and an omission. In Kübler's apparatus to p. 47,5, Mai's reading is 'assem sibi τυροῦ porrigentem' (genitive), not τυρόν. The reviewer also leaves out that Kübler's text reads 'assem sibi tyrum porrigentem'. Manuscripts A and P both have 'assem'; P omits 'tyrum'; A has 'saturum' and P 'saturnum' for Satyrum; Eberhard conjectures 'caseum'. None of this affects the note.

Source line of note 53, 'Iul. Val. 1,35 (Kübler 1888, pp. 45–47)'. The chapter numbers follow Müller, which is the project's convention; context.json says 'Iul. Val. 1,35 (Müller XXXV) = Kübler cap. 35–36'. In Kübler's own numbering, chapter 35 runs from 45,27 to 46,15 (oracle, first repulse, envoy dream). Chapter 36 runs from 46,16 to 47,14 (letter, torture, satyr dream, sack, Tripolis). The same applies to note 54: the letter is Kübler cap. 36, p. 46,16-28. For clarity the source line could read 'Iul. Val. 1,35 (Kübler cap. 35–36, pp. 45–47)'. It is not wrong under the Müller convention.

An optional precision for the Tripolis clause. Valerius says the three villages had helped Alexander in the war: 'quorum navo auxilio ad operam bellicam usus erat' (Kübler 47,12-13). In α they help open the gates: 'μετὰ τῶν τριῶν κωμῶν ... συμμαχομένων ... ἤνοιξαν τὰς πύλας' (Kroll 40,10-12) and 'τὰς δὲ τρεῖς κώμας τὰς συμμαχησαμένας αὐτῷ' (40,14-15). The note could say «из трёх деревень, помогавших ему в войне» / 'from three villages that had helped him in the war'. The current wording is not wrong.

An observation, not an error in note 53. The Epitome (ch. 34, 'classi iussa sese apud Tripolim opperiri'), Valerius (Kübler 43,24) and α 1.34 (Kroll 37) all name Tripolis as the fleet's meeting point before it is founded at Tyre (Kübler 47,13; Kroll 40,15). The Epitome inherits this anachronism; a note could mention it if wanted.

The rest of note 53 checks out against Valerius: the oracle (46,5-8), the envoy dream (46,13-15), the torture to find out which envoy was Alexander (46,28-47,2), the lack of a motive in the Epitome, and the Tripolis founding (47,11-14). The note's 'запирают ворота' / 'shut their gates' is a fair paraphrase of 'moenibus clausis (obseratis A) ab ingressu oppidi arcere Alexandrum obfirmaverunt' (46,3-4).

issues.evidence: Simple agreement error. In note 8 RU the subject of the verb is «расположение», which is neuter, so the verb must be «осталось», not «остался». The content of the note is correct: Valerius has Nectanebo say «Quin ergo deprome vel tuam vel Philippi genituram» and then «Nectanabus statim suam quoque adhibet constellationem exploraturus, an illa cum Olympiadis genitura conveniret voluntatisque potiretur» (Kübler 1888, p. 3, ll. 23–27).

issues.final_text: she calls the man to her and tells him the vision of the dream.
issues.evidence: The Latin is «hominem ad se vocat, eique somnii retulit visionem» (source/book1.la.json ch. 6; Zacher p. 8). The present-perfect switch is in the Latin, but in English 'calls … and told' inside one coordinated clause reads as a slip. The fix 'calls … tells' matches the Russian «зовёт … и рассказывает» and the EN's habit of keeping historic presents elsewhere (ch. 4 'he brings out tablets', ch. 14 'Olympias at once turns again … and consults'). 'called … told' would also be correct and would suit the rest of ch. 6 EN, which is in the past ('He said', 'The queen agreed'). The reviewer's version is the closer match to the RU, so I accept it.

issues.final_text: not only royal honours but regard for him as a father
issues.evidence: Kübler 1888, p. 5, ll. 12–15: «'Si,' inquit, 'harumce nuptiarum cepero experimentum conceptuque sim potita, honor regalis tibi a regina non deerit, inque te patris adfectum fore mihi iam spes promittit.'» Olympias is speaking about her own feeling toward Nectanebo ('in te … mihi'), and that feeling is the one a person has for a father. The Greek α 1.6 confirms the direction: «τιμήσω σε … καυχήσομαι δέ σε ὡς καὶ πατέρα τοῦ παιδὸς τυγχάνοντα» (Kroll 1926, p. 7, ll. 12–13), and β (Kroll's apparatus) has «χρήσομαί σοι ὡς πατέρα τοῦ παιδίου τυγχάνοντα». In English, 'a father’s regard' naturally means the regard a father feels, which is the wrong direction, so the reviewer is right. However, the proposed 'the regard due to a father' adds a sense of obligation ('due') that is not in 'adfectus'. 'regard for him as a father' gives the right direction and matches the RU «отношение как к отцу» word for word. Minor point: 'patris' is Kübler's correction. The palimpsest T reads 'patri' (Kübler p. 5, app. to l. 15: «15 patri T.»).

issues.final_text: сев на ложе
issues.evidence: Epitome: «ingreditur Alexander amica sollicitudine, considensque lectulo» (Zacher p. 24, l. 9). Zacher's apparatus shows no epitome manuscript with ad-: «9. consedensque A. lecto LD.» Valerius: «ingreditur amica sollicitudine tunc Alexander adsidensque lectulo» (Kübler p. 24, ll. 25–26; app. «asidensque P»). 'adsidere' + dative is the standard sickbed idiom: L&S s.v. assideo B 2 «Of the sick, to attend upon … adsidet aegrae, Ov. H. 20, 137 … habes qui Adsideat, Hor. S. 1, 1, 82». 'considere' takes no dative of the thing one sits beside. L&S s.v. consido: «constr. with in and abl., sub and abl., ante, the simple abl., or absol.» Its examples of the plain ablative all mean 'on': «transtris, Verg. A. 4, 573», «solio medius consedit avito, id. A. 7, 169», «mecum saxo, Ov. M. 1, 679», «tergo tauri, id. ib. 2, 869». Georges also cites «in lecto alcis [considere], Val. Max.» The epitome uses the verb the same way in ch. 11: «gallina in sinum eius supersiliens considensque enixa est ovum» (Zacher p. 14, ll. 3–4), which the translation itself renders «усевшись» / 'settled there'. The scene allows it: Philip has just been laid «lectulo», and sitting on the edge of a sick man's bed is natural. The Greek gives no help, because α has no sitting at all: «Μετὰ δὲ ἡμέρας εἰσέρχεται πρὸς τὸν πατέρα καὶ λέγει» (Kroll p. 21). So «у ложа» renders Valerius, not the epitome. «присев на ложе» would also be good Russian.
sources: Zacher 1867, p. 24, l. 9 and app.; p. 14, ll. 3–4
Lewis & Short s.v. consido, assideo; Georges s.v. consido (via Logeion, University of Chicago)

issues.final_text: sitting down on the couch
issues.evidence: Same evidence as issue 11. 'considensque lectulo' (Zacher p. 24, l. 9; no manuscript has ad-) is 'considere' with a plain ablative of place, which means 'sit down on' (L&S s.v. consido: «the simple abl.», e.g. «considite transtris», Verg. Aen. 4.573). 'by the couch' renders Valerius' «adsidensque lectulo» (Kübler p. 24, l. 26), the sickbed idiom of 'adsidere' + dative. The EN already renders the epitome's 'considens' as 'settled there' in ch. 11. 'the couch' refers back correctly to 'laid him on a couch' earlier in the chapter.

The grammar point is right: 'currus' as the object of 'comprehendit' is accusative plural, and all the epitome manuscripts have it. Zacher p. 34, l. 13 has «currus quidem atque arma regalia», and his apparatus records no 'currum' (only D: «Currus quoque atque regalia arma»). The conclusion is wrong, though. The phrase is copied word for word from Valerius, and there it means Darius' own chariot. (1) Two lines earlier Valerius has Darius hide that one chariot: «currum quidem in loca quaedam abdendum mandat et avertendum, ipse autem equo conscenso properantiae consulit» (Kübler p. 54, ll. 24–27). He then writes «animosius insecutus currus quidem armaque regalia matremque … comprehendit» (p. 55, l. 3). 'quidem' picks up the earlier 'currum quidem'. (2) Valerius is translating α 1.41: «καὶ τὸ μὲν ἅρμα αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰ τόξα καὶ τὴν μητέρα καὶ τὴν γυναῖκα καὶ τὰ τέκνα … [κατέλαβεν]» (Kroll p. 47, ll. 7–8). The Greek is singular, 'his chariot'. 'currus quidem' renders 'τὸ μὲν ἅρμα αὐτοῦ', and 'arma regalia' renders 'τὰ τόξα'. Just before, α has «τὸ μὲν ἅρμα καταλείψας ἵππον ἀναβὰς ἔφυγεν» (p. 47, l. 5), and the epitome's 'amisso curru' follows this. (3) The historical tradition also has the one royal chariot: Arr. Anab. 2.11.6 «τὸ μέντοι ἅρμα τοῦ Δαρείου ἔλαβε καὶ τὴν ἀσπίδα … καὶ τὸ τόξον»; Plut. Alex. 20.10 (Perrin) 'he did take the king's chariot, and his bow'. (4) Using the plural 'currus' for one chariot is ordinary poetic usage, which the archaizing Valerius takes over. Georges s.v. currus: «Plur. currus v. einem Wagen, Verg. Aen. 1, 486; 6, 485». Compare Verg. Aen. 6.485 «Idaeumque etiam currus, etiam arma tenentem» (Priam's charioteer, chariot and arms together, as here) and Ov. Met. 2.47 «currus rogat ille paternos». In the epitome, chariots captured during the pursuit of the king himself, right after 'amisso curru', would make no sense. The reviewer also says the singular is unmarked. It is not: the translator's doubts already flag it (review/book1-for-review.md, ch. 41: «‘currus’ may be accusative plural (‘chariots’); after ‘amisso curru’ the royal chariot is meant»). Keep «захватил колесницу и царское оружие». The doubt should be strengthened and a sentence added to note 64 (exact texts in other_findings).
sources: Verg. Aen. 1.486, 6.485; Ov. Met. 2.47 (The Latin Library)

issues.evidence: Same as issue 19. 'currus' is accusative plural in form, but it is Valerius' poetic plural for Darius' single chariot. Valerius: «currum quidem in loca quaedam abdendum mandat» (Kübler p. 54, ll. 24–25) and then «currus quidem armaque regalia … comprehendit» (p. 55, l. 3). This renders α «τὸ μὲν ἅρμα αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰ τόξα» (Kroll p. 47, l. 7). Compare Arr. 2.11.6 «τὸ μέντοι ἅρμα τοῦ Δαρείου ἔλαβε … καὶ τὸ τόξον», Plut. Alex. 20.10 'the king's chariot, and his bow', and, for the plural of one chariot, Verg. Aen. 6.485 «currus, etiam arma tenentem». The epitome keeps the sense with 'amisso curru' just before. 'the chariots' would turn the capture of the king's chariot and arms into a capture of the army's chariots, which neither source has. Keep 'captured the chariot and the royal arms'. 'his chariot' is unnecessary: the reference back to 'having lost his chariot' is clear. The singular is already flagged in the doubts list, so the reviewer's 'unmarked' is inaccurate. The recommended doubt and note texts are in other_findings.

issues.final_text: И так, примерно на третий день,
issues.evidence: Epitome: «Atque ita tertia fere die, conlapsis omnibus quae obstabant» (Zacher p. 36, ll. 3–4). Valerius: «Atque ita tertio fere die conlapsis omnibus, quae obstabant» (Kübler p. 62, l. 19). With numbers and times, 'fere' means 'about'. L&S s.v. fere: «quinta fere hora, about the fifth hour, Cic. Pis. 6, 13 … tertia fere vigilia, Caes. B. G. 4, 23, 1». Georges: «bes. bei Zahlen- u. Zeitangaben, ungefähr, so ziemlich». «почти на третий день» implies the third day had not yet come, and it is also not idiomatic Russian. The EN 'on about the third day' is right, and «примерно» brings the RU into line with it. The Greek has «Ἐντὸς μὲν οὖν τριῶν ἡμερῶν … ἡ Θηβαίων ἐπυρπολεῖτο πόλις» (Kroll p. 54, l. 4), so it gives no reason to read 'almost' either.
sources: Lewis & Short and Georges s.v. fere (via Logeion)

other_findings: Ch. 14, reviewer's separate view on 'Qui dum sedulo huius artis peritia frueretur, iamque se in hisce doctum perpenderet' (Zacher p. 19, l. 2): I agree that Alexander is the better reading and that nothing needs correcting. 'Qui' attaches to the nearest name, 'Alexandro' (dative, previous line). 'iam … doctum' describes a pupil who now thinks himself trained. The epitomator is reworking Valerius' «Enim non una sedulitas discenti puero cum magistro» (Kübler p. 15, ll. 9–10), where the zeal ('sedulitas' → 'sedulo') belongs to the learning boy ('discenti puero' → 'se doctum'). This is indirect support for Alexander, somewhat stronger than the reviewer allows. A Nectanebo reading is not impossible: it would make an ironic link with 'Conquerendum tibi erat de arte, quam noveras', but 'iam' makes it weak.

Ch. 14, 'assidenti sibi Alexandro … loqueretur' (Zacher p. 18, l. 11; app.: «Qui cum B Vac. adsidente Vac.», so only the Valerius witnesses have -e): I agree with the reviewer. Valerius has the ablative absolute «Qui cum adsidente sibi Alexandro ex arte illa astrica loqueretur, interpellat puer» (Kübler p. 14, ll. 26–27). The epitome's -i is the usual late spelling of the participial ablative. The present RU «в присутствии сидевшего рядом Александра» and EN 'with Alexander sitting beside him' are therefore sound. A dative reading ('speaking to Alexander, who sat beside him') is grammatically possible, but the context is against it, because Olympias has just consulted Nectanebo. No change needed.

Ch. 14, the doubts list does not match the text in two places. (a) The doubt on 'Qui dum sedulo…' gives the choice as «пока тот прилежно пользовался его знанием…», but the RU text reads «И пока тот [Александр] усердно пользовался знанием этого искусства». «его знанием» would also suggest a different construal. The doubt should quote the text as printed. (b) The doubt on 'Conquerendum tibi erat' gives the choice as ‘It is the art… that you ought to complain of’, but the EN text reads 'You ought to have complained about the art that you had known.'

Ch. 41, recommended replacement for the translator's doubt on 'currus quidem atque arma regalia'. Issue: ‘currus’ is formally accusative plural (all manuscripts; Zacher p. 34 app.). It is copied from Valerius, where it is Darius’ own chariot: just before, Darius orders ‘currum quidem … abdendum’ (Kübler p. 54), and Valerius is rendering α ‘τὸ μὲν ἅρμα αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰ τόξα’ (‘his chariot and his bow’, Kroll p. 47). It is a poetic plural for one chariot, as in Verg. Aen. 6.485 ‘currus … arma tenentem’. Choice: ‘the chariot and the royal arms’ / «колесницу и царское оружие».

Ch. 41, recommended sentence to add at the end of the first sentence group of note 64. RU: «Слово «currus», которым названа захваченная затем колесница, — форма множественного числа; она взята у Валерия, который так передаёт греческое «τὸ μὲν ἅρμα αὐτοῦ» («его колесницу», α 1.41).» EN: «The word for the chariot Alexander then captures, ‘currus’, is plural in form; it comes from Valerius, who uses it to render the Greek ‘τὸ μὲν ἅρμα αὐτοῦ’ (‘his chariot’, α 1.41).» Add to the note's source: «Ps.-Call. α 1.41 (Kroll 1926, p. 47)». Note also that the epitome's 'amisso curru' is closer to α's «τὸ μὲν ἅρμα καταλείψας» (Kroll p. 47, l. 5) than to Valerius' 'abdendum mandat'. This could support the note's 'in the Epitome he has “lost” it'.

Ch. 22, suggested new doubt entry, since the translation now departs from Valerius. Latin: «considensque lectulo». Issue: Valerius has ‘adsidensque lectulo’ (sitting by the sickbed, the usual sense of ‘adsidere’ + dative); the epitome changed the verb. ‘considere’ with a bare ablative means ‘to sit down on’ (Verg. Aen. 4.573 ‘considite transtris’; cf. ch. 11 ‘in sinum eius supersiliens considensque’). The Greek α 1.22 has no sitting. Choice: «сев на ложе» / ‘sitting down on the couch’.

Note 11 (ch. 6): 'patris adfectum' is Kübler's correction. The Turin palimpsest, the only witness cited there, reads 'patri' (Kübler p. 5, app. to l. 15: «15 patri T.»). Optionally write ‘patris adfectum’ (Kübler; T ‘patri’). The Greek quotation is accurate: Kroll p. 7, l. 13 has «καυχήσομαι δέ σε ὡς καὶ πατέρα τοῦ παιδὸς τυγχάνοντα». β in Kroll's apparatus reads «χρήσομαί σοι ὡς πατέρα τοῦ παιδίου τυγχάνοντα».

Ch. 6 EN, minor: 'for while you are sitting, a serpent will come crawling upon you' for «sedenti superveniet draco reptabundus». 'crawling upon you' can be read as crawling over her body. 'superveniet' means 'will come up to / arrive upon' her, and the RU is «к тебе приползёт змей». Suggested wording: 'a serpent will come crawling up to you'.

issues.final_text: В эпитоме этого оракула нет. Помета Кролля «om. Val.» (с. 3, к строкам 10–18) здесь не независимое свидетельство: текст Валерия в этом месте утрачен, и Кюблер печатает вместо него эпитому (см. схолию 1). Был ли этот оракул здесь у Валерия, неизвестно; но в 1,34 Валерий приводит его как надпись под статуей Нектанеба (царь вернётся «не старше, а моложе»), и Александру объясняют, что этот оракул был дан египтянам, когда они искали своего царя.
issues.evidence: The reviewer is right in substance. (1) Kübler's text at this point is the Epitome. In the Conspectus notarum (unnumbered page after praef. p. XXXI) Kübler says: 'Libri primi caput primum et initium capitis secundi supplevi ex Epitoma a Zachero edita.' Kübler p. 2, ll. 1–8 ('Igitur ad consuetam artis confugit peritiam ... cum magna admiratione commendabat') is word for word Zacher ch. 3 (Zacher p. 3, ll. 6–13). The app. on p. 2, to 2,9 reads: 'verba longe celebratior incipiunt ea, quae legi in codice rescripto Taurinensi.' Even l. 11 'lateret. Coepitque supplevi ex Epitoma'. No other Valerius manuscript covers this point. On P, praef. pp. XXIII–XXIV: 'incipit Iulius Valerius a verbis in id, quod cupiverant commeatus (p. 6,27) ... Desunt igitur ... capita I–VII libri primi Iulii Valerii, quae quod quidem sciamus non servantur nisi in codice Taurinensi.' A begins at 'ad votum proclivitas' (p. 20,24; praef. p. XXIII and app. p. 20). Kroll's preface says the Göttingen leaves cover only p. 4,16–7,22 and 14,2–17,10 (praef. p. VIII n.). (2) Kroll's apparatus, p. 3, reads exactly '10—18 om. Val.' Lines 10–18 run from 'Ἐν δὲ τῇ Αἰγύπτῳ ἀφανοῦς γενομένου τοῦ Νεκτανεβῶ' to 'εἰς μνήμην ποτὲ τοῦ ἐκβησομένου τοῦ χρησμοῦ': the whole oracle episode, including the inscription on the statue base. Line 19, 'Ἐν δὲ τῇ Μακεδονίᾳ φανερὸς γίνεται', corresponds to Valerius' 'Ergo iam longe celebratior', where T begins. So 'Val.' at 10–18 can only mean the Epitome text that Kübler printed. Kroll does the same on p. 2: his app. there cites 'Alanos Val.', 'Ozydracontas Val.' and 'Val, qui de suo add. Phoenicesque Parthos et Assyrios'. In Kübler all of these stand in the Epitome-supplied ch. 1. (3) The oracle does appear later in Valerius. Kübler p. 44, ll. 8–13 (Valerius 1,34 in the project's Müller numbering; Kübler's ch. 33, Müller XXXIV): 'statuam quandam nigro lapide intuetur cum illa super Nectanabo inscriptione, imperatorem scilicet eum, qui fuga indidem abfuisset, rursus Aegyptum reventurum, non seniorem, enim iuniorem, eumque fore loci illius hostium subiugatorem.' Lines 17–18: 'Tum sese quaerentibus civibus oraculum datum, quod sub illa statua legeretur.' This is exactly the α 1.3 episode, told in retrospect. Whether Valerius had also told it at 1,3 cannot be decided. T's 'Ergo iam' after the gap settles nothing either way. The reviewer's fix is correct but drops the useful fact that Valerius knows the oracle. My text keeps that fact, ties 'om. Val.' to its place in Kroll, and keeps 'не старше, а моложе' as in note 51. The source line of note 5 should add: Kübler 1888, p. 2 app. (to l. 9); Iul. Val. 1,34 (Kübler p. 44, ll. 8–18).

issues.final_text: The oracle is absent from the Epitome. Kroll’s ‘om. Val.’ (p. 3, on lines 10–18) is not independent evidence here: Valerius’ text is lost at this point, and Kübler prints the Epitome in its place (see note 1). Whether Valerius had the oracle here cannot be known; but in 1,34 he gives it as the inscription beneath Nectanebo’s statue (the king will return ‘not older, but younger’), and Alexander is told that this oracle was given to the Egyptians when they were seeking their king.
issues.evidence: Same evidence as issue 1. Kübler, Conspectus notarum: 'Libri primi caput primum et initium capitis secundi supplevi ex Epitoma a Zachero edita.' Kübler p. 2 app.: '2, 9 verba longe celebratior incipiunt ea, quae legi in codice rescripto Taurinensi.' P and A begin only at p. 6,27 and p. 20,24 (praef. pp. XXIII–XXIV). Kroll p. 3 app.: '10—18 om. Val.' This covers the whole Egyptian oracle passage; l. 19 'Ἐν δὲ τῇ Μακεδονίᾳ' = 'longe celebratior'. On p. 2 Kroll likewise cites Epitome-supplied readings as 'Val.' ('Alanos Val.', 'Val, qui de suo add. Phoenicesque ... et Assyrios'). Valerius knows the oracle: Kübler p. 44, ll. 9–13, 'rursus Aegyptum reventurum, non seniorem, enim iuniorem', and ll. 17–18, 'Tum sese quaerentibus civibus oraculum datum, quod sub illa statua legeretur'. The reviewer's EN fix is correct in substance. Mine adds the line reference and the true, relevant point about 1,34.

issues.final_text: Ср. у Плутарха (Alex. 2.6; 3.1–2): змей, которого однажды видели рядом со спящей Олимпиадой, охладил к ней Филиппа; после этого видения дельфийский оракул велел Филиппу приносить жертвы Аммону и чтить его больше всех богов и предсказал, что он лишится того глаза, которым подсмотрел в щель двери бога в облике змея на ложе своей жены.
issues.evidence: This final_text replaces the whole last sentence of note 19 ('Ср. у Плутарха (Alex. 2.6; 3.2): ... в облике змея.'), not only the quoted clause, because the citation also changes to 3.1–2. Greek (Perseus, Perrin's text, ch. 3): 'Φιλίππῳ μὲν, μετὰ τὸ φάσμα πέμψαντι Χαίρωνα τὸν Μεγαλοπολίτην εἰς Δελφοὺς, χρησμὸν κομισθῆναι λέγουσι παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ κελεύοντος Ἄμμωνι θύειν καὶ σέβεσθαι μάλιστα τοῦτον τὸν θεόν· ἀποβαλεῖν δὲ τῶν ὄψεων αὐτὸν τὴν ἑτέραν, ἣν τῷ τῆς θύρας ἁρμῷ προσβαλὼν κατώπτευσεν ἐν μορφῇ δράκοντος συνευναζόμενον τῇ γυναικὶ τὸν θεόν.' The δέ-clause with ἀποβαλεῖν answers θύειν καὶ σέβεσθαι, so it is part of what the god's oracle said. Formally ἀποβαλεῖν could be taken with λέγουσι ('they say that he lost'), which is probably where 'будто бы лишился' came from. But the standard translations all take it as the oracle's content. Perrin (LacusCurtius 3.1–2): 'who bade him sacrifice to Ammon ... 2 but told him he was to lose that one of his eyes'. Stewart and Long (Gutenberg #14140): 'warning him, moreover, that he would some day lose the sight of that eye'. Dryden/Clough (Gutenberg #674): 'was told he should one day lose that eye'. Plutarch says nothing about the prophecy coming true. The next sentence turns to Olympias: 'ἡ δὲ Ὀλυμπιάς, ὡς Ἐρατοσθένης φησί ...' (3.3 in Perrin's numbering). So in Alex. 3 the eye is only a prediction (a divine sentence), not a narrated fact. The reviewer's fix is right. I add three things: it is the Delphic oracle; it also ordered honour to Ammon, which matters here because ch. 10 ends with Olympias naming Ammon; and Philip spied through the chink of the door. Section numbers follow Perrin's Loeb, as printed in LacusCurtius: serpent 2.6, oracle 3.1–2. The Perseus Greek file uses coarser sections (2.4; 3.1). The 2.6 part of the note is right: 'ὤφθη δέ ποτε καὶ δράκων κοιμωμένης τῆς Ὀλυμπιάδος παρεκτεταμένος τῷ σώματι· καὶ τοῦτο μάλιστα τοῦ Φιλίππου τὸν ἔρωτα καὶ τὰς φιλοφροσύνας ἀμαυρῶσαι λέγουσιν'.

issues.final_text: Compare Plutarch (Alex. 2.6; 3.1–2): a serpent once seen lying beside the sleeping Olympias cooled Philip towards her; after this apparition the Delphic oracle told Philip to sacrifice to Ammon and revere him above all gods, and foretold that he would lose the eye with which he had spied through the chink of the door on the god, in serpent form, lying with his wife.
issues.evidence: This final_text replaces the whole last sentence of note 19 ('Compare Plutarch (Alex. 2.6; 3.2): ... in serpent form.'). Same evidence as issue 8. Greek: 'χρησμὸν κομισθῆναι λέγουσι παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ κελεύοντος Ἄμμωνι θύειν καὶ σέβεσθαι μάλιστα τοῦτον τὸν θεόν· ἀποβαλεῖν δὲ τῶν ὄψεων αὐτὸν τὴν ἑτέραν, ἣν τῷ τῆς θύρας ἁρμῷ προσβαλὼν κατώπτευσεν ...' (Perseus ch. 3). Perrin's Loeb (LacusCurtius 3.2): 'but told him he was to lose that one of his eyes which he had applied to the chink in the door'. Plutarch passes straight to Olympias and Eratosthenes and does not say the prophecy came true. So 'he is said to have lost the eye' misstates the passage. The reviewer's fix is correct. Mine adds Delphi and Ammon, the chink of the door, the reason for the timing ('μετὰ τὸ φάσμα') and the corrected citation 3.1–2.

issues.final_text: Когда скорлупка раскололась, было видно, как из неё вышел змеёныш.
issues.evidence: Zacher p. 14, ll. 5–6: 'Cuius testula dissultante visus est de ea dracunculus exisse.' The Epitome reworks Valerius, Kübler p. 10, ll. 13–15: 'cuiusque testula dissultante dracunculus, ut pote tantilli conclavis pertenuis, egredi visitur'. 'visitur' means 'is seen', not 'seems'. The context treats the event as something actually seen. Valerius p. 10, l. 17: 'Ea visio non parvum scrupulum Philippo in animum iniecerat'; ll. 20–21: 'aperit rem visitatam: gallinam, ovum, dracunculum'. The Epitome itself, Zacher p. 14, l. 10, has 'super re visa sciscitans'. The Greek α 1.11 tells it as plain fact (Kroll p. 11): 'ἀφ᾽ οὗ ἐξεπήδησε μικρὸν δρακόντιον'. 'visus est' is the usual passive 'was seen' of prodigy reports. «показалось» wrongly suggests an illusion. The EN 'was seen to come out' is already right. The fix also matches the translator's own rendering in ch. 1 of 'moveri ac vivere visebantur' as «было видно, как оно движется и оживает».

other_findings: Note 19, first sentence (RU «чтобы супружеской верности ничего не недоставало» / EN 'so that nothing should be lacking to conjugal fidelity') gets the sense wrong. Valerius (Kübler p. 9, ll. 22–26) reads: 'genibus sinuque mulieris insidens promptum os porrigit et cum bisulco linguae vibratu osculum uxoris adfectat, ne quid omnino coniugali fidei deesset apud eum maritum, cui talis visio proderetur.' Here 'fides' means proof or credibility, as in 'quo fidem faceret divino commercio' (ll. 18–19), and the clause is about convincing the husband who sees it. The Greek α agrees: 'τεκμήριον στοργῆς ... πρὸς τοὺς θεωμένους καὶ αὐτὸν τὸν Φίλιππον' (quoted in Zacher p. 13 app.; Kroll p. 10 app.). 'Fidelity' says the opposite of what is meant. Also, the serpent does not 'touch her' with its tongue; it 'seeks a kiss' ('osculum adfectat'). And Philip draws back 'una metu unaque admiratione', in fear and amazement at once (l. 26). Suggested first sentence. RU: «У Валерия (1,10) змей ещё усаживается Олимпиаде на колени и, трепеща раздвоенным языком, тянется её поцеловать, «чтобы в глазах мужа, которому явлено такое зрелище, достоверности этого супружества ничего не недоставало» (ne quid omnino coniugali fidei deesset apud eum maritum, cui talis visio proderetur), а Филипп отступает в страхе и изумлении; эпитоматор это выпустил.» EN: 'In Valerius (1,10) the serpent also settles on Olympias’ knees and, flickering its forked tongue, tries to kiss her, ‘so that, in the eyes of the husband to whom such a sight was shown, nothing should be lacking to the credibility of the union’ (ne quid omnino coniugali fidei deesset apud eum maritum, cui talis visio proderetur), while Philip draws back in fear and amazement; the epitomator omitted this.'

Note 19, the 'sobrius' point is correct: 'Tunc ex admiratione sobrius Philippus' (Kübler p. 9, l. 29) against the Epitome's 'Tunc ex admiratione Philippus exhilaratus' (Zacher p. 13, ll. 4–5). Kroll's app. p. 10 shows the Greek behind 'sobrius': 'ὁ δὲ Φίλ. ἐκ τοῦ φόβου νοήσας (ἀνανήψας B′ ...)'. This could be added if wanted.

Note 51 (ch. 34), RU «(как и оракул о возвращении в гл. 3)» / EN '(as he dropped the oracle of the return in ch. 3)', assumes Valerius had the oracle in ch. 3. That cannot be known, because Valerius is lost there (see issue 1). Suggested wording: RU «(в гл. 3 эпитомы этого оракула тоже нет)» / EN '(the Epitome has no oracle of the return in ch. 3 either)'. Note 51 could also say that in Valerius Alexander is told the oracle was given to the citizens seeking their king ('Tum sese quaerentibus civibus oraculum datum, quod sub illa statua legeretur', Kübler p. 44, ll. 17–18).

Note 5, source line: add 'Kübler 1888, p. 2 app. (to l. 9); Iul. Val. 1,34 (Kübler p. 44, ll. 8–18)'. Note that Kübler numbers this chapter 33, with Müller's XXXIV in his margin; the project's '1,34' follows Müller.

Note 4 (ch. 2) words it carefully as 'an addition of the Latin text' and is right to do so. Kroll's p. 2 app. ('Val, qui de suo add. Phoenicesque ... et Assyrios') attributes to Valerius words that survive only in the Epitome, which Kübler printed in ch. 1. If the note is ever reworded, it should not attribute this to Valerius.

Ch. 11, last sentence, RU «И поскольку змей, как видно, вырвался из него» for 'Ex quo cum draco erupisse videatur' (EN 'since the serpent was seen to break out of it'). «Как видно» reads as 'apparently, evidently' and repeats on a small scale the problem of issue 10. Optional, for consistency: «И поскольку видели, как змей вырвался из него, обошёл весь круг этой округлости, пожелал войти туда, откуда произошёл, и умер прежде, чем это сбылось, — ясно, что…». Valerius has the same 'videatur' in Antiphon's speech (Kübler p. 10, ll. 28–29).

issues.final_text: В рукописях эпитомы эти числа записаны большей частью римскими цифрами (словами лишь изредка, например «octo» в L, «octingentos» в A и B); Цахер печатает все числа словами.
issues.evidence:
The reviewer is right that not every word form is Zacher's. Two details are wrong. (1) The print has octingentos in A and B, not A and E. The archive.org OCR misreads 'ABVb' as 'AEYb'; I checked the page image. (2) Vb is not an Epitome manuscript. Zacher p. VIII–IX: 'Vb = Mailand, Ambrosiana, Part. sup. P. 49 … Nach dem Frankfurter abdrucke … von A. Mais erster ausgabe'. That is the Milan manuscript of Valerius.

Zacher p. 27, apparatus to ll. 21–23 (checked in the image): '26. 21. … x̄v. HLABD. milia fehlt LDE. 22. … in octo mil. L. in .viii. mil. B. in .viii. mil. AE. .i. viii. mil. H. in fehlt D. .xviii. D. .ii. dccᵗᵒˢ HLAB. .ii. dcc. E. 23. septingentos et duo milia Vb. .v. dcc. D.'

Zacher p. 28, apparatus to l. 1: 'octingentos ABVb. dcccᵗᵒˢ H. dccc. DE. dcc. L.' Apparatus to l. 3: '.lxx dcᵗᵒˢ iiii. mil militantium H. .lxx. dc. iiii. militantium LAE. .dc. lxx. iiii. militantium B. lxx. d. iiii. D. .dcliiii. ad .lxx. milia militantium erant Vb. „In Taur. desunt quinquaginta.“ Mai.'

What each Epitome manuscript (H L A B D E) has, number by number:
- quindecim: numerals (x̄v) in H L A B D. E is not reported, so by Zacher's silence it has the word.
- octo: the word in L only; numerals in A B E H D.
- duo milia septingentos: numerals in all six.
- octingentos: the word in A and B; numerals in H D E, and L has 'dcc', an error.

So 'mostly numerals' is accurate. The reviewer's fix is right in substance; mine names the attested word forms.

The rest of note 46 holds:
- 15,000 + 8,000 + 2,700 + 800 = 26,500.
- The Epitome's 'septuaginta milia sexcentos quatuor' (Zacher p. 28, ll. 2–3) is 70,604.
- Kübler p. 30, ll. 22–23 prints 'sexcenti quinquaginta quattuor ad septuaginta milia militantium erant', i.e. 70,654. His apparatus to l. 22 reads '22 DCIV T. Epit.'. His conspectus notarum defines T as 'lectiones codicis rescripti Taurinensis', the Turin palimpsest.

issues.final_text: The Epitome manuscripts mostly give these figures in Roman numerals (only occasionally in words, e.g. ‘octo’ in L, ‘octingentos’ in A and B); Zacher prints them all in words.

So the word is in A and B, not A and E (E has DCCC), and Vb is the Milan manuscript of Valerius, not of the Epitome (Zacher p. VIII–IX). Zacher p. 27, apparatus to l. 22 has 'in octo mil. L.', so L has octo in words. Everything else in ch. 26 is in numerals in all the Epitome manuscripts, except quindecim in E (by Zacher's silence). issues.final_text: Перевод («при стольких силах») следует чтению эпитомы «consitum»; чтение «confisum» означало бы «полагающийся на такие силы».
issues.evidence:
Zacher p. 31, apparatus to l. 24 (checked in the image): 'totque viribus — consitum HLABE. Vinc. Bell. tot tribub; — consitum D. hisce viribus consitum Vb. hisce viribus confisum Müll. τηλικαύτῃ δυνάμει ἐπαιρόμενον ALBC. ἐπερόμενον cod. Florent.' So all six Epitome manuscripts have consitum. Vb, the Milan manuscript as printed by Mai, also has consitum: Zacher p. VIII says his Vb readings come from 'dem Frankfurter abdrucke (Francof. 1818) von A. Mais erster ausgabe'. Müller has confisum.

Kübler p. 50, l. 5 (checked in the image): 'tantum regem Darium et hisce viribus confisum, deorum, ut praedicat, consessorem'. His apparatus to l. 5 has only '5 his viribus P. deorumque P.', so he records no variant for confisum. Kübler praef. p. XXII, on the Ambrosianus: 'a me collatus anno 1885'. Kroll α 1.38: 'τηλικαύτῃ δυνάμει ἐπαιρόμενον'. All the factual statements of note 59 hold.

On the reviewer's point: the note itself glosses consitum as 'здесь «снабжённый»'. «При стольких силах» expresses having the forces, not relying on them, so it renders consitum. Confisum adds the king's attitude, trust in his forces, which is also the sense of the Greek ἐπαιρόμενον; the translation does not convey that. So 'подходит к обоим чтениям' is wrong, and the reviewer is right. Following consitum is correct, because the Epitome manuscripts all have it. The reviewer's «на столькие силы» is awkward Russian. My version uses «на такие силы», matching the EN 'such forces', and puts the Latin words in «» as the rest of the note does.

issues.final_text: The translation (‘furnished with such forces’) follows the Epitome’s reading ‘consitum’; ‘confisum’ would mean ‘relying on such forces’.
issues.evidence: The evidence is the same as for issue 17. Zacher p. 31, apparatus to l. 24 has 'consitum HLABE … consitum D … hisce viribus consitum Vb. hisce viribus confisum Müll.' Kübler p. 50, l. 5 has 'hisce viribus confisum', and his apparatus to l. 5 records no variant for it ('5 his viribus P. deorumque P.'). 'Furnished' is exactly the sense the note gives for consitum ('here ‘furnished’'). It does not render confisum, 'relying on, trusting in', which is close to the Greek ἐπαιρόμενον, 'elated by' (Kroll α 1.38). So 'suits both readings' is wrong, and the reviewer's substance is right. I changed only two things: the Latin words are quoted, as elsewhere in the note, and I added 'the Epitome’s reading' to show why consitum is followed.

- Arrian, Anab. 1.11.3 (Perseus text, Roos): 'τὰ μὲν κατὰ Μακεδονίαν τε καὶ τοὺς Ἕλληνας Ἀντιπάτρῳ ἐπιτρέψας'.

other_findings: Ch. 38, translator's doubts: the entry for 'totque viribus, ut sese iactat, consitum' says 'Rendered neutrally: ‘furnished with such forces’ / «при стольких силах»'. After the fix to note 59 this contradicts the note. Suggested: 'Rendered after the Epitome’s consitum: ‘furnished with such forces’ / «при стольких силах»; see note.'

Note 59, 'так что «consitum», возможно, ошибка Маи' / 'so ‘consitum’ may be Mai’s error': this rests only on Kübler's silence. The note's own first clause points the other way. All six Epitome manuscripts (H and L are 9th c.) have consitum, and they are independent of Mai, whose 1817 edition used only the Ambrosianus (Kübler praef.: 'uno codice Ambrosiano usus'). So consitum was already in the Valerius text the epitomator used. Mai and the Epitome making the same error by chance is unlikely, so Kübler may simply have failed to record the variant. A fairer wording: RU 'так что неясно, ошибся ли Маи или Кюблер не отметил разночтения; эпитома во всяком случае показывает, что «consitum» — старое чтение.' EN 'so it is unclear whether Mai erred or Kübler failed to record the variant; the Epitome at least shows that ‘consitum’ is an old reading.'

Note 59 says confisum is 'Müller's reading'. That is accurate, but Kübler's silence at p. 50, l. 5 implies the Paris manuscript (Kübler's P) also has confisum. Zacher p. IX says one can rarely tell whether Müller's departures from Mai come from the Paris manuscript or are his own emendations. So 'Müller's reading' should not be taken as 'Müller's conjecture'. No change is needed if the wording stays neutral.

Note 46 (optional): Zacher p. 28, apparatus to l. 3, supports the note independently. It gives the Milan manuscript of Valerius (Vb, from Mai) as '.dcliiii. ad .lxx. milia militantium erant' and quotes Mai: '„In Taur. desunt quinquaginta.“'. One Epitome manuscript, D, has 'lxx. d. iiii.' (70,504). This is not an error in the note.

Note 66 (optional): Zacher p. 35, apparatus to l. 1, 'moliebatur — Scamandrum fehlt E': Zacher's best manuscript, E, leaves out the whole clause naming Scamander. It could be added if the note is meant to give the evidence for the name in full.

Reviewer's method: for issues 13–14 the reviewer relied on the archive.org OCR, which misreads 'ABVb' as 'AEYb' on Zacher p. 28. The reviewer also counted Vb, the Milan manuscript of Valerius, among the Epitome manuscripts. Other apparatus claims in this review that rest only on the OCR are worth checking against the page images.

issues.final_text:
A wax figure inscribed with a name has a parallel in the Graeco-Egyptian magical papyri: the erotic binding spell PGM IV 296–466 prescribes modelling two wax figures, a man and a woman, writing on the woman’s breast the name of the woman to be bound, together with her mother’s name, and reciting a spell. The little bed, the lamps and the herbal juice have no counterpart in this recipe.
(source: PGM IV 296–466 (Preisendanz 1928, I, pp. 82–89))
issues.evidence:
Same evidence as issue 4, from Preisendanz, PGM I (1928).

- Greek, p. 82, IV 296–297: 'λαβὼν κηρὸν ⟨ἢ πηλὸν⟩ ἀπὸ τροχοῦ κεραμικοῦ πλάσον ζῴδια δύο, ἀρρενικὸν καὶ θηλυκόν'.
- Apparatus, p. 82: '296 κηρον P, was Rieß hält; πηλὸν Kt'. The papyrus reads wax; 'or clay' is an editorial supplement, so the reviewer's 'wax or clay' overstates the papyrus.
- IV 317–318: 'ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ στήθους τὸ ὄνομα τῆς ἀγομένης μητρόθεν'. German, p. 83: 'auf die Brust den Namen der Beigezwungenen nach ihrer Mutter'.
- The spell is written on a lead tablet and recited (IV 329–335).
- The deposit is made at the grave of someone untimely or violently dead (IV 333–334).
- There is no bed, lamps or herbal juice anywhere in IV 296–466 (pp. 82–89).

The reviewer's EN fix ('two figures made of wax or clay … a parallel for the wax figure') is correct in spirit. It loses the name-on-the-figure parallel, which the papyrus does support, and it treats the supplement as text.
sources: Preisendanz, Papyri Graecae Magicae I (Leipzig 1928), pp. 82–89: https://archive.org/details/papyrigraecaemag0001unse_x4f6

issues.final_text:
RU (replaces the sentence «Сравнений с Пегасом и конями Лаомедонта в A нет, но Пегас есть в β … касается лишь придаточного о конях Лаомедонта.»):
Сравнений с Пегасом и конями Лаомедонта в A нет. Пегас есть в β (L B C: κάλλει διαφέροντα τοῦ Πηγάσου) и в армянской версии: там конь превосходит «красотой и быстротой» Пегаса и Ариона, а привели его, по словам приведших, «из Ламоментеа» — вероятно, это искажённое имя Лаомедонта. Значит, сравнение с Пегасом восходит к греческому источнику, а упоминание Лаомедонта, по-видимому, тоже; замечание Цахера «вся эта фраза отсутствует в греческих текстах ALBC» касается лишь придаточного о конях Лаомедонта.

EN (replaces the corresponding sentence 'The comparisons with Pegasus … concerns only the clause about Laomedon’s horses.'):
The comparisons with Pegasus and Laomedon’s horses are missing in A. Pegasus is in β (L B C: κάλλει διαφέροντα τοῦ Πηγάσου) and in the Armenian version, where the horse surpasses Pegasus and Arion ‘in beauty and speed’ and is said to have been brought ‘from Lamomentea’, probably a garbled form of Laomedon’s name. So the Pegasus comparison goes back to the Greek source, and the mention of Laomedon probably does too; Zacher’s remark that ‘this whole phrase is absent from the Greek texts ALBC’ concerns only the clause about Laomedon’s horses.

Source line: (source: Ps.-Call. α 1.13 (Kroll 1926, p. 14 with app.); β: Müller 1846, Ps.-Call. p. 13; Armenian text, Venice 1842, p. 16 (§ 31); Iul. Val. 1,13 (Kübler 1888, pp. 12–14); Zacher 1867, p. 17 app.)
issues.evidence:
β is confirmed three ways:
- Zacher 1867, p. 17 app., lemma 6: 'κάλλει διαφέροντα τοῦ Πηγάσου (πηγάσου L.) LBC. fehlt A.'
- Müller 1846 (Didot, Ps.-Callisthenes), p. 13, I.13 text from B: 'τοῦτον τὸν ἵππον ἐν τοῖς βασιλικοῖς ἱπποφορβίοις εὕρομεν γεννηθέντα, κάλλει διαφέροντα τοῦ Πηγάσου'. Note 23 adds that C has 'τῷ μὲν κάλλει διαφέροντα τοῦ Πηγάσου, τῇ δὲ γνώμῃ δράκοντος ἀνημέρου'.
- Kroll 1926, p. 14 app. ad l. 15, checked against the page image: 'in B′ Arm. equisones oratione directa utuntur, dicentes equum κάλλει (καὶ τάχει add. Arm.) διαφέροντα τοῦ Πηγάσου (κ. τοῦ Ἀρεινος Arm.); cf. Val. qui add.: et si equi fuisse Laomedontis eiusmodi praedicantur'. B′ is Kroll's siglum for recension β (B C M L F V). His Armenian readings come from Raabe's Greek retroversion (praef. p. VIII).

Armenian text: I read it myself from the page image of the Mekhitarist edition (Venice 1842; archive.org patmutiwnagheks00pseugoog), p. 16, § ԼԱ (31). My transcription: 'գեղեցկութեամբ եւ արագութեամբ առաւել քան զՊեգասոս եւ քան զԱրիովնայն. զի եւ ’ի Լամոմենտեայ բերեալ մատուցանեմք քեզ' ('surpassing in beauty and speed Pegasus and Arion; and we have brought it from Lamomente-a and offer it to you'). This agrees with Kroll's 'καὶ τάχει' and 'κ. τοῦ Ἀρ[ί]ονος'.

So the Armenian has Pegasus (plus Arion and 'speed'). It names Laomedon only if 'Lamomente-' is taken as a garbled Laomedont-, which is plausible but conjectural. Nothing in it corresponds to 'mares', so 'кобылицы Лаомедонта' is not supported.

Zacher, p. 17 app., lemma 7, after the Turin palimpsest reading 'equi fuisse Laomedontis eiusmodi praedicantur': 'Diese ganze phrase fehlt in den griechischen texten ALBC'. The note's reading of this remark is correct.

I could not check Raabe 1896 for § 31. The Belgrade University Library scan (CC BY) kept resetting the connection, and I got only as far as Raabe p. 7 (I.10–12). The HathiTrust copies sit behind a bot check, which I did not try to pass. I also did not consult Stoneman–Gargiulo 2007 or Wolohojian 1969, since only restricted or unauthorised copies are online. So 'Lamomentea = Laomedon' should stay hedged ('вероятно').

RU (note 36): «Исторически Филипп женился на Клеопатре, племяннице македонского вельможи Аттала, в 337 г. до н. э.»; (note 38): «В основе сцены — свадьба 337 г. до н. э.» EN (note 36): 'Historically Philip married Cleopatra, niece of the Macedonian noble Attalus, in 337 BC.'; (note 38): 'Behind the scene lies the wedding of 337 BC.'
issues.evidence:
The ancient evidence only brackets the date:
- Plutarch, Alex. 9.2–11 (Perrin, Loeb VII, via LacusCurtius) puts the wedding after Chaeronea (Aug. 338). 9.2: 'He was also present at Chaeroneia …'; then 9.6: 'The most open quarrel was brought on by Attalus at the marriage of Cleopatra …'.
- Diodorus 17.2.3 (Welles, LacusCurtius): 'Cleopatra had borne a child to Philip a few days before his death' (summer 336).
So the wedding falls in late 338 or 337.

The standard date is 337. Smith, Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology, s.v. Cleopatra (3) (Perseus): 'Philip married her when he divorced Olympias in B. C. 337'. Ogden's chapter in the Cambridge Companion to Alexander the Great (2024, pp. 42–54) is reported in search results to date it 'probably early 337', but I could not open the full text (paywalled), so I do not rely on it.

No hedge is needed in a margin note. If more caution is wanted, the only defensible alternative is 'в 338/337 г.' I could not check modern handbooks (Bosworth 1988, Heckel 2006): only restricted lending copies are online.

The details of note 38 match Plutarch 9.7–10 ('Attalus, now, was the girl's uncle'; Alexander 'threw a cup at him'; Philip 'rose up against him with drawn sword, but … his anger and his wine made him trip and fall').
sources: Smith, Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology, s.v. Cleopatra (3): https://cts.perseids.org/read/pdlrefwk/viaf88890045/003/perseus-eng1/C.cleopatra_3
Ogden, 'Crises leading up to Alexander's accession', Cambridge Companion to Alexander the Great (2024), doi:10.1017/9781108888349.003 (abstract only seen)

issues.final_text: No change. RU (note 52): «…Нектанеб II потерял Египет при Артаксерксе III около 343 г. до н. э. и бежал в Эфиопию (Диодор, 16, 51, 1).» EN: '…Nectanebo II lost Egypt to Artaxerxes III c. 343 BC and fled to Ethiopia (Diodorus 16.51.1).'
issues.evidence:
The flight is confirmed by Diodorus 16.51.1 (Sherman, Loeb, via LacusCurtius): 'So giving up hope of his kingship and taking with him the greater part of his possessions, he fled into Aethiopia.'

The date: Ruzicka, Trouble in the West: Egypt and the Persian Empire 525–332 BC (Oxford 2012), ch. 'Persian Success, 344–342', abstract: 'Artaxerxes finally succeeded in reconquering Egypt in 343/2.' Livius.org gives the Persian arrival as 'the last months of 343'.

There is a minority dating. Depuydt, 'New Date for the Second Persian Conquest, End of Pharaonic and Manethonian Egypt: 340/39 B.C.E.', Journal of Egyptian History 3.2 (2010) 191–230, argues for 340/339. Ruzicka (2012) still uses 343/2.

'Около 343 г.' / 'c. 343 BC' is the standard date and already hedged, so it can stand. A more exact wording, if wanted, is 'в 343/342 г. до н. э.' / 'in 343/342 BC'.

Note that Diodorus himself narrates the campaign under the archonship of Thessalus (16.40.1, i.e. 351/0). So the citation supports the flight, not the year.

other_findings: Issues 4–5 of the review cite studylib.net (https://studylib.net/doc/27838760/...) for Betz's translation. That is an unauthorised copy and should not be cited anywhere in the apparatus or the review record. Use Preisendanz 1928 (archive.org) or the printed Betz instead.

Issues 4–5: the reviewer's 'two figures of wax or clay' treats Preisendanz's supplement ⟨ἢ πηλόν⟩ as papyrus text. The papyrus reads only κηρόν (apparatus, p. 82: '296 κηρον P, was Rieß hält; πηλὸν Kt').

Note 24 also leaves out that the Armenian adds 'and speed' (καὶ τάχει) and a second horse, Arion (Kroll p. 14 app.: 'κ. τοῦ Ἀρεινος Arm.'; the edition's 'Ἀρεινος' is evidently meant for Ἀρίονος/Ἀρείονος). Its 'mares of Laomedon' (кобылицы) has no basis in the Armenian text. Unless the Stoneman–Gargiulo citation can be checked in print, I suggest replacing it in the source line with the checked sources.

Note 52 cites Diodorus 16.51.1 next to the date 343. Diodorus himself puts the reconquest under the archon year 351/0 (16.40.1), so the citation supports the flight to Ethiopia, not the year. This is acceptable as written, but the date comes from modern chronology.
Note 36 follows Plutarch (Alex. 9.7) in making Attalus Cleopatra's uncle. Diodorus 17.2.3 calls him her brother. No change is needed; the conflict could be mentioned if the note is expanded.
